Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.
item.dc:creator: K\"ur\c{s}at \c{C}akal, Suat \"Ozdemir

item.title: Execution Logs Sway VLM Judges of Robot Progress
item.description: arXiv:2610.34151v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models now grade robot videos, and text placed beside the frames can change their verdicts. On clips where the robot is losing progress, we add one log line saying the robot is making progress. Across Gemini, Qwen and GPT judges, this flips correct verdicts to progress 10 to 35 percentage points more often than a neutral line does. A one-line warning that the log may be wrong removes most of this effect. Selected fake "task complete" claims flip half of Qwen's correct verdicts, against a tenth for unrelated log lines. They have no detectable effect on Gemini.
item.dc:creator: Weiyan Zhao, Sunny Yang

item.title: Robust Single-Parameter Point Cloud Registration using Truncated Lp Functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.34271v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a novel method for robust point cloud registration with only one tunable parameter. Our method, dubbed TLP, uses truncated $L_p$ functions with different values of $p$ to assign priority scores to correspondences, select the hypothesis, and refine the final model. By leveraging the robustness of truncated functions, TLP effectively handles the high outlier rates commonly encountered in real-world 3D feature matching. We also exploit GPU parallelization to evaluate hypotheses efficiently, enabling registration from thousands of correspondences in under a second on average. With only one tunable parameter, our method offers greater practicality than multi-parameter methods that require dataset-specific tuning of several parameters. Evaluations on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that TLP achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art single-parameter methods. Furthermore, it outperforms two widely used multi-parameter methods on three of the four evaluated datasets while maintaining competitive runtime.
item.dc:creator: Seong Hun Lee, Patrick Vandewalle, Javier Civera

item.title: EAST: Embodied AI Safety Testing via Systematic Fault Injection in Digital Twins
item.description: arXiv:2610.34358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Task success is not a sufficient measure of safety for embodied artificial intelligence (AI), because robots may complete objectives while violating safety requirements. Existing evaluations often emphasize performance and robustness, but lack a systematic route from documented safety hazards to executable, verifiable tests. We present EAST (Embodied AI Safety Testing), a digital-twin framework that converts literature-grounded safety evidence into fault-injection tests across perception, instructions, environments, actions, and timing. EAST combines an expert-reviewed safety-fault taxonomy and eight executable operators with applicability and validity constraints. Its three-stage workflow generates test specifications, verifies fault realization during simulated execution, and independently assesses safety challenges, violations, task outcomes, and behavioral signatures using simulator-state evidence. The framework preserves execution traces and replayable records, supporting attribution and reproducibility across experiments. We evaluate EAST on six RoboTwin manipulation tasks and two policy architectures, ACT and RDT, against alternative testing strategies under matched budgets. Across five comparative campaigns, EAST targets all 74 admissible task-policy-operator combinations and obtains valid evidence for 63, while achieving safety-challenge exposure rates close to Random-Legal and Rule-Based. Moreover, 82 valid EAST executions complete their tasks despite safety violations, revealing risks concealed by success-oriented evaluation. These findings support systematic, validity-aware, reproducible safety testing beyond task-completion metrics.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Tian, Tao Li, Ling Zhou, Dave Towey, Zhaoxin Fan, Wenjun Wu, Rubing Huang, Tsong Yueh Chen

item.title: Nonlinear Control of Aerial Manipulator
item.description: arXiv:2610.34454v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents two controllers for a quadrotor equipped with a two-DOF robot manipulator that physically interacts with the environment. Cartesian impedance and adaptive sliding mode controllers are implemented and compared for a simple hovering task in the presence of some bounded disturbance. A full dynamic model is developed, and the two above controllers are implemented with the same initial conditions and desired position.
item.dc:creator: Sandesh Thapa

item.title: Trajectory Generation and Control for Quadrotors
item.description: arXiv:2610.34456v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this project, I explored controller design and trajectory generation for a quadrotor. Differential flatness was used for trajectory generation based on one of the references. A minimum snap trajectory is generated from the given algorithm based on waypoint navigation, and a simple proportional plus derivative (PD) controller is used to track the trajectories. Simulation results are presented which generate smooth trajectories for position and velocity of the quadrotor.
item.dc:creator: Sandesh Thapa

item.title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Hierarchical Exploration Captures Future Volitional Action in Drosophila
item.description: arXiv:2610.34638v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.
item.dc:creator: Declan Kutscher, Reece Keller, Alyn Kirsch, Felix Pei, Aran Nayebi

item.title: Video World Models Need Predictable Latents
item.description: arXiv:2610.34663v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video world models trained on large-scale robot data promise a safe and scalable approach for learning and evaluating policies that act in the physical world. However, they still struggle with long-horizon rollouts and out-of-distribution generalization, and they remain computationally demanding at inference time. Typically, video world models make predictions in the latent space of a reconstruction-trained autoencoder, which however is not directly optimized for dynamics modeling. On the other hand, world models designed for latent planning usually optimize latents to be predictable, but they forgo accurate prediction of observations in pixel space. In this paper, we show that it is possible to achieve the best of both worlds: a latent geometry optimized to make future prediction as simple as possible without sacrificing accurate prediction of future observations. More precisely, we find that temporal objectives for representation learning, paired with a past-conditioned decoder architecture, lead to consistent improvements in generative video world models at the same training budget. The gains include up to 5x cheaper inference, over 7x faster training, and 15-24% lower pixel and perceptual errors out of distribution and over long horizons. Our world models also agree more closely with real-world policy evaluation when using a vision-language model to judge task success from their pixel-space predictions. Overall, our study indicates that temporal predictability is an important design criterion for the latent space of video world models, and provides concrete guidance on how to incorporate it into the training of autoencoders.
item.dc:creator: Mattia Scardecchia, Sherry Yang

item.title: DriveUniTok: A Unified Multimodal Tokenizer for Driving World-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.35044v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
item.dc:creator: Jingbo Xu, Hanchao Leng, JiaHui Huang, Hanbing Li, Jingwei Zhao, Kuiyuan Yang, Chen Gao, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Yong Li

item.title: Uncertainty Evaluation to Support Safety of the Intended Functionality Analysis for Determining the Applicability of Performance Targets Across Triggering Conditions in ML-Based LiDAR Object Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.35092v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) analysis according to ISO 21448, a machine learning object detector for light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds can meet a performance target, a limit on the mean per-frame share of wrong detections among accepted detections, by rejecting detections above an uncertainty threshold. A threshold selected on data of one condition carries a statistical guarantee only for data distributed like its selection data, whereas SOTIF analysis covers every triggering condition. This paper presents an uncertainty evaluation in which the threshold is transferred into a triggering condition, a test decides at a stated error probability whether the target is applicable there, not applicable or not determined, and a lower bound counts the independent units an applicable outcome requires. For PointPillars ensembles on KITTI and nuScenes, counted in recorded sequences, as the dependence between frames requires, neither dataset held enough independent units for any target limit, and no transfer had a not applicable outcome. Counted in frames, the same data gave not applicable outcomes at limits fixed in advance after transfers into far distance, into rain and between two separately trained detectors, thresholds that met the target limit after a transfer rejected most correct detections, and in rain the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve did not decrease. A performance target met under one condition therefore counts as evidence under a triggering condition only after a test there, reported with its share of accepted correct detections and its number of independent recorded sequences.
item.dc:creator: Milin Patel, Rolf Jung

item.title: High-resolution tactile observation makes hidden racket-control mechanisms learnable
item.description: arXiv:2610.35563v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Experts can master fine hand-object manipulation skills, yet limited conscious perception of rapid tactile interactions hinders their ability to articulate the underlying control mechanisms. Badminton racket control requires rapid, fine hand-force coordination, providing a demanding testbed for uncovering these mechanisms. An 864-node tactile-inertial glove with synchronized 100-Hz acquisition recorded over 14,000 strokes from more than 70 participants across five skills. Inspired by sensorimotor control, our mechanics-grounded two-layer framework inferred object-driving and grip-stabilizing control from tactile history, while resolving their spatiotemporal force realization. We found that higher proficiency was associated with selective rather than extensive control: greater skill specificity, anticipatory regulation, focal distal modulation and lower geometric torque cancellation, while spatiotemporal coordination showed a non-monotonic acquire-refine pattern. We translated these mechanisms into personalized guidance targeting force control and force-motion coordination. In a randomized cohort, mechanism-guided learners gained 0.72 expert-rated skill levels versus 0.05 with level-only feedback, making control mechanisms actionable.
item.dc:creator: Haoyang Tian, Zhengwei Li, Houcheng Li, Xu Yang, Peigeng Gu, Xinyue Wang, Tairan Zhu, Shuo Jiang, Long Cheng

item.title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.
item.dc:creator: Akshay Mete, Dileep Kalathil, P. R. Kumar

item.title: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Using Routed Ensembles and Trajectory Attribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.35733v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning is a fundamental problem for modern AI, with applications spanning post-training, reasoning models, and robotic control. A central challenge is to learn policies that balance competing objectives, such as helpfulness versus honesty in safety and alignment, or speed versus energy in robotics. The optimal policy can vary sharply with objective-weighting combinations, and the extent of this variation depends crucially on the degree of conflict among objectives, making per-preference policy learning sample-inefficient. In this paper, we introduce objective-conflict coefficients and derive near-optimal regret bounds for online settings using this measure, thereby quantifying the impact of misalignment on learning efficiency. Then, we design routed ensemble policy learning, an algorithm that maintains a small set of basis policies and dynamically routes trajectories to the policy with the highest potential reward. Finally, we consider trajectory selection as another approach to mitigate objective conflict, and design a kernel surrogate trajectory attribution algorithm that estimates how feedback signals from a set of trajectories influence policy learning on other trajectories. The kernel can capture nonlinear interactions such as synergy and antagonism between trajectories. We evaluate our approach across diverse environments and benchmarks: routed ensembles improve average performance by 4.3% over baselines for online environments from Meta-World and MO-Gymnasium, and kernel surrogate attribution improves correlation with leave-one-out analysis over existing baselines by 50%. When applied to trajectory selection, kernel-based attribution yields a 27% improvement in reward over baseline attribution methods.
item.dc:creator: Zhenshuo Zhang, Ruoxuan Xiong, Hongyang R. Zhang

item.title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35850v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
item.dc:creator: Guowen Zhang, Liyi Chen, Xu Hu, Pengfei Wang, Jingfan Chen, Chenhang He, Lei Zhang

item.title: Nonprehensile Robotic Catching Using Virtual Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.35851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The problem of nonprehensile robotic catching is addressed using virtual nonholonomic constraints (VNHCs); the motion of the robot end-effector is designed and controlled directly in terms of the states of the object before it is caught on the surface of the end-effector. In contrast to contemporary approaches, our approach avoids the need for object trajectory prediction, and consequent time-varying robot trajectory generation. With a focus on the planar case, we demonstrate that our VNHC approach can be used to catch an object on an end-effector at a desired height, with minimal relative normal velocity at the contact instant. Moreover, the VNHC function depends only on the desired catching height, and the same VNHC can be used for a range of initial conditions. We use model predictive control (MPC) to bring the object and end-effector to rest at a desired location after contact is made. The approach is validated in simulation.
item.dc:creator: Aakash Khandelwal, Ranjan Mukherjee

item.title: Making Space for Time: The Special Galilean Group and Its Application to Some Robotics Problems
item.description: arXiv:2409.14276v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The special Galilean group, usually denoted SGal(3), is a 10-dimensional Lie group whose important subgroups include the special orthogonal group, the special Euclidean group, and the group of extended poses. We briefly describe SGal(3) and its Lie algebra and show how the group structure supports a unified representation of uncertainty in space and time. Our aim is to highlight the potential usefulness of this group for several robotics problems.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Kelly

item.title: Automotive-ENV: Benchmarking Multimodal Models in Automotive Cockpit Environments
item.description: arXiv:2509.21143v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal models have demonstrated strong capabilities in web, desktop, and mobile GUI environments, but their performance in automotive cockpit systems remains largely unexplored. In-vehicle GUIs introduce unique challenges beyond traditional GUI interaction, including vehicle-state reasoning, implicit intent understanding, and safety-critical decision making. To address this gap, we introduce Automotive-ENV, an interactive benchmark for evaluating multimodal models in automotive cockpit environments. Built on Android Automotive OS, Automotive-ENV combines cockpit-screen interaction with vehicle-state signals and deterministic state-based evaluation. The benchmark contains 420 carefully constructed tasks covering routine cockpit operation and safety-critical scenarios. Unlike prior GUI benchmarks that rely on action matching or LLM-based judging, Automotive-ENV evaluates model behavior through reproducible validators over UI states, vehicle signals, and safety-related conditions. We benchmark representative general-purpose multimodal models and GUI-specialized vision-language models on Automotive-ENV. Experimental results show that current models remain far from reliable in automotive environments, with substantial performance degradation in implicit and safety-critical tasks. Further analysis reveals consistent failure modes in safety-aware reasoning, vehicle-control understanding, and implicit hazard recognition. We release Automotive-ENV, together with tasks, validators, and evaluation tools, to support future research on automotive multimodal systems.
item.dc:creator: Junfeng Yan, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Ling Chen

item.title: Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement: A Call for Body-Control Co-Design for Humanoid Robot
item.description: arXiv:2510.03081v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Humanoid robots, as general-purpose physical agents, must integrate both intelligent control and adaptive morphology to operate effectively in diverse real-world environments. While recent research primarily optimizes control policies for fixed bodies, we advocate body-control co-design as a path toward physical Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI): using experience from a humanoid's current body and policy to guide successive improvements to both. Inspired by biological evolution, this approach enables robots to recursively adapt both their form and behavior to optimize performance within task-specific and resource-constrained contexts. Despite its promise, co-design in humanoid robotics remains a relatively underexplored domain, raising fundamental questions about its feasibility and necessity in achieving true embodied intelligence. To address these challenges, we discuss potential co-design methodologies grounded in strategic exploration, Sim2Real transfer, and meta-policy learning. We further argue for the essential role of co-design by analyzing it from methodological, application-driven, and community-oriented perspectives. Striving to guide and inspire future studies, we present open research questions, spanning from short-term innovations to long-term goals. Ultimately, co-design offers a path toward physical RSI in humanoids that improves their bodies and policies while learning to make this improvement process more effective.
item.dc:creator: Guiliang Liu, Bo Yue, Yi Jin Kim, Kui Jia

item.title: A Shared Control Framework for Mobile Robots with Planning-Level Intention Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2511.08912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In mobile robot shared control, effectively understanding human motion intention is critical for seamless human-robot collaboration. This paper presents a novel shared control framework featuring planning-level intention prediction. A path replanning algorithm is designed to adjust the robot's desired trajectory according to inferred human intentions. To represent future motion intentions, we introduce the concept of an intention domain, which serves as a constraint for path replanning. The intention-domain prediction and path replanning problems are jointly formulated as a Markov Decision Process and solved through deep reinforcement learning. In addition, a Voronoi-based human trajectory generation algorithm is developed, allowing the model to be trained entirely in simulation without human participation or demonstration data. Extensive simulations and real-world user studies demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces operator workload and enhances safety, without compromising task efficiency compared with existing assistive teleoperation approaches.
item.dc:creator: Jinyu Zhang, Lijun Han, Feng Jian, Lingxi Zhang, Hesheng Wang

item.title: IndustryNav: Evaluating Spatial Reasoning and Safety of Embodied Agents in Dynamic Industrial Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2511.17384v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual large language models (VLLMs) are increasingly used as embodied agents, yet industrial warehouses demand more than reaching a goal: agents must navigate safely around moving workers and vehicles. To evaluate embodied agents' goal reaching and safety, we introduce IndustryNav, a simulation environment with 24 warehouse scenes for closed-loop navigation to specified destinations. Alongside task success and efficiency, we introduce safety-aware metrics that capture collisions and near-collision warnings along each trajectory. Experiments with eleven leading open- and closed-source VLLMs and three navigation baselines show that agents can reach their goals yet collide with moving obstacles, exposing a gap between success and safe navigation. This gap matters in safety-critical settings, where a single collision can end the task. IndustryNav also supports policy learning through automated oracle trajectories and simulator interaction, with held-out scenes for generalization tests. These experiments show that policies can succeed on new routes in familiar warehouses yet fail to transfer to held-out layouts, making cross-scene generalization an open challenge.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Li, Lichi Li, Anh Dao, Xinyu Zhou, Wenjun Huang, Tianyi Ma, Yicheng Qiao, Zheda Mai, Daeun Lee, Zichen Chen, Pan Wang, Lehan Yang, Tianlong Wang, Zhen Tan, Sheng Li, Mohit Bansal, Yang Ni, Yu Kong

item.title: Guardian: Detecting Robotic Planning and Execution Errors with Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2512.01946v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robust robotic manipulation requires reliable failure detection and recovery. Although recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) show promise in robot failure detection, their generalization is severely limited by the scarcity and narrow coverage of failure data. To address this bottleneck, we propose an automatic framework for generating diverse robotic planning and execution failures across both simulated and real-world environments. Our approach perturbs successful manipulation trajectories to synthesize failures that reflect realistic failure distributions, and leverages VLMs to produce structured step-by-step reasoning traces. This yields GuardianFail-36k, a large-scale failure reasoning dataset built upon the RLBench simulator and the BridgeDataV2 real-robot dataset. Using GuardianFail-36k, we train Guardian, a multi-view reasoning VLM for unified planning and execution verification. Guardian achieves state-of-the-art performance on three unseen real-world benchmarks: RoboFail, RoboVQA, and our newly introduced UR5-Fail. When integrated with a state-of-the-art LLM-based manipulation policy, it consistently boosts task success rates in both simulation and real-world deployment. These results demonstrate that scaling high-quality failure reasoning data is critical for improving generalization in robotic failure detection. Code, Data, and Models are available at https://www.di.ens.fr/willow/research/guardian/.
item.dc:creator: Paul Pacaud, Ricardo Garcia, Shizhe Chen, Cordelia Schmid

item.title: CRAFT-E: An Interpretable and Editable Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Affordance-Grounded Active Object Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2512.04231v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Assistive robots operating in unstructured environments must reason not only about what objects are, but how they can be used, including non-canonical and improvised uses. This requires grounding language-based action queries to objects that afford the requested function, are visually present, and can be physically retrieved. Existing approaches often rely on black-box models, fixed affordance labels, or direct object predictions, limiting transparency and controllability. We introduce CRAFT-E, a modular neuro-symbolic framework that composes an LLM-derived verb-property-object knowledge graph with CLIP-based visual alignment and energy-based grasp reasoning. The system exposes interpretable grounding paths, incorporates grasp feasibility into affordance inference, and supports targeted graph edits without retraining. We also construct a benchmark dataset with unified annotations for verb-object compatibility, segmentation, and grasp candidates, and deploy the full pipeline on a physical robot. Across static scenes, real-world trials involving 20 verbs and 39 objects, ImageNet-based functional retrieval, and COCO-Tasks transfer, CRAFT-E provides a competitive training-free prior for affordance-grounded retrieval while exposing component-level diagnostics and graph-level interventions. Under staged and full-pipeline perception, CRAFT-E matches strong flat LLM priors in several settings while adding failure attribution and editable reasoning paths. By coupling symbolic reasoning with embodied perception, CRAFT-E offers an inspectable and customizable framework for affordance-grounded object retrieval.
item.dc:creator: Zhou Chen, Joe Lin, Carson Bulgin, Sathyanarayanan N. Aakur

item.title: Collaborative Continuum Robots: A Survey from an Automation-System Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2601.10721v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuum robots (CRs), owing to their compact structure, inherent compliance, and flexible deformation, have been widely applied in various fields. By coordinating multiple CRs to form collaborative continuum robots (CCRs), task adaptability, flexibility and load capacity can be further improved, thus offering significant advantages. In recent years, interest in this emerging field has grown steadily within the continuum-robotics community. In this survey, a closed-loop task-execution architecture for CCRs is constructed from an automation-system perspective, clarifying the system-level logic that transforms target-task specifications into multi-CR collaborative execution. Based on this architecture, CCRs are classified into three representative collaboration modes, namely separated collaboration, assistance collaboration, and parallel collaboration. Research progress is then systematically summarized and analyzed in terms of key technologies, including multi-CR task allocation, structural design, modeling, motion planning methods, control strategies, and sensing mechanisms. Finally, research opportunities in key technologies and system integration challenges for real-world deployment are discussed, providing guidance for research and application of CCRs.
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Li, Qian Tang, Guoxin Yin, Gang Zheng, Jessica Burgner-Kahrs, Cesare Stefanini, Ke Wu

item.title: DWPP: Dynamic Window Pure Pursuit Considering Velocity and Acceleration Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2601.15006v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pure pursuit and its variants are widely used for mobile robot path tracking owing to their simplicity and computational efficiency. However, many conventional approaches do not explicitly account for velocity and acceleration constraints, resulting in discrepancies between commanded and actual velocities that result in overshoot and degraded tracking performance. To address this problem, this paper proposes dynamic window pure pursuit (DWPP), which fundamentally reformulates the command velocity computation process to explicitly incorporate velocity and acceleration constraints. Specifically, DWPP formulates command velocity computation in the velocity space (the $v$-$\omega$ plane) and selects the command velocity as the point within the dynamic window that is closest to the line $\omega = \kappa v$. Experimental results demonstrate that DWPP avoids constraint-violating commands and achieves superior path-tracking accuracy compared with conventional pure pursuit methods. The proposed method has been integrated into the official Nav2 repository and is publicly available (https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2).
item.dc:creator: Fumiya Ohnishi, Masaki Takahashi

item.title: UniManip: Open-World Robotic Manipulation via Agentic Operational Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2602.13086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Achieving general-purpose robotic manipulation requires robots to bridge high-level semantic intent with low-level physical interaction in unstructured environments. However, zero-shot generalization remains challenging: end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often lack the precision required for long-horizon tasks, while traditional hierarchical planners suffer from semantic rigidity under open-world variations. We present UniManip, a unified framework centered on an Agentic Operational Graph (AOG), an explicit cognitive and operational backbone for task orchestration, state tracking, execution verification, and closed-loop failure recovery. High-level semantic intents are grounded into actionable primitives via a physically grounded scene graph that provides geometric affordances, contact-aware interaction parameters, and collision-free trajectory synthesis. By coupling a high-level Agentic Layer for task orchestration with a low-level Scene Layer for dynamic state representation, UniManip continuously aligns abstract planning with geometric constraints, enabling robust execution. Unlike static pipelines, UniManip operates as a dynamic agentic loop: it instantiates object-centric scene graphs from unstructured perception, parameterizes these representations into collision-free trajectories via a safety-aware local planner, and exploits structured memory to autonomously diagnose and recover from execution failures. UniManip achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO-Pro, while extensive real-world experiments demonstrate robust zero-shot generalization across diverse tasks, embodiments, and dexterous hands, outperforming leading VLA models and hierarchical baselines by 22.5% and 25.0% in task success rate, respectively. Open-source project page: https://henryhcliu.github.io/unimanip.
item.dc:creator: Haichao Liu, Yuanjiang Xue, Yuheng Zhou, Li Yang, Haoyuan Deng, Yinan Liang, Lihua Xie, Ziwei Wang

item.title: FlowHOI: Flow-based Semantics-Grounded Generation of Hand-Object Interactions for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2602.13444v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate plausible end-effector motions, yet they often fail in long-horizon, contact-rich tasks because the underlying hand-object interaction (HOI) structure is not explicitly represented. An embodiment-agnostic interaction representation that captures this structure would make manipulation behaviors easier to validate and transfer across robots. We propose FlowHOI, a two-stage flow-matching framework that generates semantically grounded, temporally coherent HOI sequences, comprising hand poses, object poses, and hand-object contact states, conditioned on an egocentric observation, a language instruction, and a 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) scene reconstruction. We decouple geometry-centric grasping from semantics-centric manipulation, conditioning the latter on compact 3D scene tokens and employing a motion-text alignment loss to semantically ground the generated interactions in both the physical scene layout and the language instruction. To address the scarcity of high-fidelity HOI supervision, we introduce a reconstruction pipeline that recovers aligned hand-object trajectories and meshes from large-scale egocentric videos, yielding an HOI prior for robust generation. Across the GRAB and HOT3D benchmarks, FlowHOI achieves the highest action recognition accuracy and a 1.7$\times$ higher physics simulation success rate than the strongest diffusion-based baseline, while delivering a 40$\times$ inference speedup. We further demonstrate real-robot execution on four dexterous manipulation tasks, illustrating the feasibility of retargeting generated HOI representations to real-robot execution pipelines.
item.dc:creator: Huajian Zeng, Lingyun Chen, Jiaqi Yang, Yuantai Zhang, Fan Shi, Peidong Liu, Xingxing Zuo

item.title: RoboGene: Diversity-Driven Agentic Task Generation Framework for VLA Pre-training
item.description: arXiv:2602.16444v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection incurs prohibitive physical costs. The key challenge is thus not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain informative training data that broadens behavioral coverage across objects, scenes, and skills. Yet automatically curating task proposals to maximize the utility of collected data remains under-explored. We introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework for generating diverse, informative manipulation tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. RoboGene combines (1) diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, (2) agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and (3) human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and continual refinement. Through quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, we collect 18k trajectories and introduce metrics for task feasibility and diversity. RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro. VLA models trained on RoboGene-generated data achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the value of high-quality task generation. Project page: https://robogene-boost-vla.github.io/. Datasets: Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/X-Humanoid/RoboGene) and ModelScope (https://modelscope.cn/datasets/X-Humanoid/RoboGene_tasks).
item.dc:creator: Yixue Zhang, Kun Wu, Zhi Gao, Zhen Zhao, Pei Ren, Zhiyuan Xu, Fei Liao, Xinhua Wang, Shichao Fan, Di Wu, Qiuxuan Feng, Meng Li, Zhengping Che, Chang Liu, Jian Tang

item.title: Prepare to Turn: Learning Anticipatory Maneuvering for Fast Sequential Quadrupedal Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2603.12842v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast quadrupedal navigation requires preparing for the next turn while approaching the current goal. Policies trained to reach and remain at a single target can instead produce stop-and-go motion when applied to sequential goals, compromising its agility potential. We introduce PrepTurn, a reinforcement learning framework for anticipatory maneuvering in sequential local navigation. PrepTurn maps the current and next pose goals directly to joint actions, using the upcoming goal to inform how the robot should approaches the current one. Its persistent-credit reward encourages timely completion of the whole sequence by continuing to reward reached goals while moving on and preparing subsequent maneuvers, and an automatic curriculum that gradually increases goal difficulty is critical for learning stable turning behaviors. Together, these components enable the policy to coordinate approach speed and reorientation across goal transitions without prescribed trajectories or arrival times. Simulation and onboard Unitree Go2 experiments demonstrate fast, efficient sequential traversal with high completion and reduced stop-and-go motion. We further show that when the goal-reaching tolerances are more relaxed, the policy learns to exploit the freedom allowed by the task with emergent behaviors, such as turning to the next goal in advance and cutting corners within the permitted regions behaviors, to traverse goal sequences more efficiently.
item.dc:creator: Zunzhi You, Yunke Wang, Haolan Guo, Chang Xu

item.title: ArrayTac: A Closed-Loop Piezoelectric Tactile Platform for Continuously Tunable Rendering of Shape, Stiffness, and Friction
item.description: arXiv:2603.13829v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human touch depends on the integration of shape, stiffness, and friction, yet existing tactile displays cannot render these cues together as continuously tunable, high-fidelity signals for intuitive perception. We present ArrayTac, a closed-loop piezoelectric tactile platform that simultaneously renders these three tactile dimensions with continuous tunability on a 4 by 4 actuator array. Each unit integrates a three-stage micro-lever amplifier with end-effector Hall-effect feedback, enabling up to 5 mm displacement, an array refresh rate greater than 500 Hz, and a closed-loop bandwidth of 123 Hz. In psychophysical experiments, naive participants identified three-dimensional shapes and distinguished multiple stiffness and friction levels through touch alone without training. We further demonstrate image-to-touch rendering from an RGB image and remote palpation of a medical-grade breast tumor phantom across a distance of more than 1,000 km, in which all 11 participants correctly identified the number and type of tumors with a sub-centimeter mean localization error. Together, these results establish ArrayTac as a programmable multidimensional tactile rendering platform that bridges digital representations, physical environments, and human tactile perception, enabling intuitive tactile communication between humans and machines.
item.dc:creator: Tianhai Liang, Shiyi Guo, Baiye Cheng, Zhengrong Xue, Han Zhang, Huazhe Xu

item.title: Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.19233v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A fine-tuned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy can easily place the alphabet soup in the basket on command, just as it saw during fine-tuning. However, if the basket is shifted five centimeters to the left, it drops the soup off the table. We developed an interpretability pipeline to investigate what such a policy is computing. Injecting task A's activations into the action expert while the policy looks at task B's scene makes pi0.5 execute task A's motor trajectory in 99.6\% of episodes ($n{=}1{,}968$). The injected program is bound to absolute workspace coordinates and ignores the visible scene, which provides a mechanistic account of the perturbation brittleness that concurrent benchmarks report. The binding holds on a physical UR10e: directed replay redirects the commanded task in 26/26 rollouts in one direction and 18/26 in the other, with no-injection and random-direction controls at the floor, and once the source object is moved 10--15\,cm the arm grasps and releases at the recorded coordinates in 50/50 trials, picking up the wrong block when one sits there and closing on empty air when none does. Applying the same interventions to six VLAs on LIBERO, MetaWorld, SimplerEnv, and ALOHA over 420{,}000+ rollouts yields three further findings: every architecture encodes the instruction, and four of the five weight it below vision whenever the scene alone identifies the goal; under the standard replacement write-back the SAE pooling that preserves behavior is architecture-specific (pi0.5 per-token, SmolVLA indifferent), and goal selection and motor generation separate into VLM and expert pathways wherever the two are distinguishable. We release \textbf{Action Atlas} (https://action-atlas.com), an interactive platform covering all 520+ trained SAEs, 79 identified concepts, and the scored UR10e rollouts. Code: https://github.com/CWRU-AISM/action-atlas
item.dc:creator: Bryce Grant, Xijia Zhao, Peng Wang

item.title: AutoWorld: Learning Multi-Agent Traffic Simulation with Self-Supervised World Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.28963v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulation with realistic traffic agents is essential for validating autonomous driving systems. Existing data-driven simulators learn agent behavior from higher-level abstractions such as 3D bounding boxes and polylines, inferred by upstream perception pipelines. These lossy abstractions discard sensory context that directly shapes agent behavior, limiting the distributional realism that simulation aims to reproduce. To address this limitation, we propose AutoWorld, a traffic simulation framework that grounds agent behavior in raw sensor observations through a self-supervised world model trained on LiDAR occupancy data. Given world model samples, AutoWorld constructs a coarse-to-fine predictive scene context as input to a multi-agent motion generation model. Furthermore, we designed a motion-aware latent supervision objective that enriches AutoWorld's latent representation of scene dynamics. To better exploit this latent space during inference, AutoWorld employs a cascaded Determinantal Point Process framework to guide diversity-aware sampling across both the world model and motion model. Experiments on nuPlan and Waymo demonstrate that AutoWorld improves generation realism, with larger gains in partially observed scenarios where trajectory abstractions are most limited, reducing collision rates by 36%. AutoWorld also remains physically plausible under planner-controlled ego behavior and supports controllable, diverse safety-critical scenario generation.
item.dc:creator: Mozhgan Pourkeshavarz, Tianran Liu, Nicholas Rhinehart

item.title: AffordSim: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark for Affordance-Aware Robotic Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2604.11674v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many everyday robot manipulation skills are affordance-dependent, with success determined by whether the robot contacts the functional object region required by the subsequent action. Current simulation data generators obtain contacts from generic grasp estimators or per-object manual contact annotations, but generic estimators rank stable grasps without task semantics and often select contacts that are misaligned with the downstream action, while manual contact annotations must be rewritten for each new object and task. To solve these challenges, we introduce AffordSim, a scalable data generator and benchmark that integrates open-vocabulary 3D affordance prediction into simulation-based trajectory generation. Given a natural-language task description, AffordSim synthesizes a task-relevant scene, emits affordance queries, grounds them on object surfaces, samples region-conditioned grasps, and selects executable candidates with motion planning. It further randomizes object pose, texture, lighting, image noise, and cross-viewpoint backgrounds for sim-to-real transfer. We instantiate AffordSim as a 50-task benchmark across diverse manipulation skills, five robot embodiments, and 500+ rigid and articulated objects. AffordSim achieves 93% of the trajectory collection success rate of manual contact annotations on affordance-critical tasks and 89% on hard composite tasks. Vision-language-action policies trained on AffordSim data transfer zero-shot to a real Franka FR3, reaching 24% average success.
item.dc:creator: Mingyang Li, Haofan Xu, Haowen Sun, Xinzhe Chen, Sihua Ren, Liqi Huang, Xinyang Sui, Chenyang Miao, Jiawei Ye, Qiongjie Cui, Xingyu Chen, Zeyang Liu, Xuguang Lan

item.title: SentryVLA: Uncertainty-Guided Action Selection and State Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Robotic Control
item.description: arXiv:2604.16677v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as generalist robotic controllers that map visual observations and language instructions to continuous actions. However, pretrained VLAs typically provide limited information about the reliability of their generated actions, making deployment challenging when execution failures must be anticipated. We address this problem by introducing SentryVLA, a lightweight runtime wrapper for frozen VLA policies. At the action level, SentryVLA uses conformalized quantile regression to estimate a calibrated upper bound on the deviation between sampled VLA actions and expert-like behavior under the calibration distribution. The predicted deviation is then used to rank multiple stochastic candidates for action selection. At the execution-monitoring level, SentryVLA applies a Mahalanobis-distance-based anomaly score to the contextualized latent execution state extracted before final action prediction, providing a complementary signal for detecting abnormal execution states during closed-loop control. The framework does not require retraining or architectural modification of the underlying VLA policy. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that SentryVLA improves action selection and provides useful runtime warning signals for abnormal execution states. These findings demonstrate the practical value of post-hoc reliability scoring for improving the runtime behavior of pretrained VLA policies. Project webpage: https://robotic-vision-lab.github.io/sentryvla/.
item.dc:creator: Zongyao Lyu, Lingling Chen, William J. Beksi

item.title: High-Speed, Scalable Sensor Readout for Dexterous Robotic Hands via Shift-Register Multiplexing
item.description: arXiv:2605.01434v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dexterous robotic hands require high-speed multimodal sensing across many degrees of freedom, yet existing readout architectures often impose trade-offs between sensor count, wiring complexity, and sampling bandwidth. This paper presents a scalable analog sensor readout architecture based on a serial-in parallel-out (SIPO) shift-register principle. The proposed architecture supports versatile integration of heterogeneous analog-output sensors, scalable expansion using only three signal lines between sensor modules, and fast, configurable sampling. We validate the approach on a tendon-driven robotic hand integrating 16 joint sensor modules and one four-channel tactile sensor module, enabling acquisition of 20 sensor channels at a full-scan rate of 1 kHz, with stable operation up to 1.5 kHz. Joint sensor characterization showed a maximum slope absolute percentage error (APE) of 0.446% and sub-degree estimation error, indicating that the proposed readout system preserves sensing performance. For tactile sensing, LSTM-based models enabled real-time force estimation and contact-location classification at 1 kHz. System-level experiments showed that the joint sensors provided more accurate feedback than motor-based estimation during interaction. Closed-loop experiments further demonstrated improved joint trajectory tracking using joint-sensor feedback and force-controlled object pinching using tactile feedback. The proposed architecture offers a practical path toward sensorized robotic hands for dexterous manipulation.
item.dc:creator: Jaehoon Kim, Boshi An, Lazaros Christoforidis, Michail Papadakis, Victor Kartsch, Robert K. Katzschmann

item.title: Visibility-Aware Mobile Grasping in Dynamic Environments
item.description: arXiv:2605.02487v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider mobile grasping in unknown and dynamic environments, where a robot must approach and grasp a target object using a camera with a limited field of view. This setting introduces two visibility constraints. Incomplete environmental observations can create collision risks along the whole-body trajectory, while occlusions can hinder object pose refinement during grasping. Previous systems often assume known or static environments and decouple perception from motion, leaving safety unresolved around unobserved obstacles. We present a unified system that enforces both visibility constraints at runtime through three core components. A velocity-aware gaze policy directs perception toward fast-moving regions of the planned swept volume, a hierarchical subgoal policy samples grasp and intermediate configurations that maintain target visibility, and a real-time whole-body planner replans over a receding horizon as the map updates. Across 400 randomized simulation scenarios and real-world trials on a Fetch mobile manipulator, our system achieves success rates of 70.4% in unknown static environments and 57.9% in dynamic environments, outperforming the decoupled navigation- and-manipulation strategy by 16.3 and 9.3 percentage points, respectively, while significantly reducing collisions.
item.dc:creator: Tianrun Hu, Anxing Xiao, David Hsu, Hanbo Zhang

item.title: A Semantic Autonomy Framework for VLM-Integrated Indoor Mobile Robots: Hybrid Deterministic Reasoning and Cross-Robot Adaptive Memory
item.description: arXiv:2605.02525v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Semantic indoor navigation requires robots to connect human instructions with spatial destinations, execute missions and retain useful operational experience. This paper presents the Semantic Autonomy Stack (SAS), a six-layer integration framework, and develops its semantic-reasoning, mission-interface and operational-memory layers over a previously validated ROS 2/Nav2 foundation. A deterministic-first cascade combines the route graph, semantic objects, robot state and stored instruction-destination associations, escalating unresolved or guarded cases to a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM). Recurrent model-mediated associations can pass a frequency-and-consistency gate and be compiled for deterministic M3 reuse; this gate measures sampled-output stability rather than semantic truth. The frozen v4.8-review implementation was evaluated on two physical robot configurations in one indoor environment, with onboard navigation and perception and shared-workstation reasoning and memory. Of 216 decision cycles outside the start gate, 112 resolved deterministically at sub-millisecond resolver-compute latency. A sealed 28-instruction challenge yielded 17 acceptable outcomes; five fast-path decisions included one incorrect selection. One promoted association was reused on the second platform through deliberate shared-digest installation. A controlled 594-observation offline comparison showed greater agreement with the stored associations and lower decision latency from M3 reuse in five familiar cases. The M3-disabled cascade reduced VLM calls but matched direct-VLM decision quality in standardized context. Large latency savings were concentrated in paths avoiding VLM inference. Together, the results establish a working integration of selective hybrid reasoning and reusable operational memory, while identifying implementation and evaluation boundaries for further development within SAS.
item.dc:creator: Bogdan Felician Abaza, Andrei-Alexandru Staicu, Cristian Vasile Doicin

item.title: BEACON: Cross-Domain Co-Training of Generative Robot Policies via Best-Effort Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2605.08571v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce BEACON--Best-Effort Adaptation for Cross-Domain Co-Training--a theory-guided framework for training generative robot policies with abundant source demonstrations and limited target demonstrations. BEACON casts cross-domain co-training as a discrepancy-aware importance-reweighting problem, jointly learning a diffusion-based visuomotor policy and per-sample source weights through an objective inspired by the Best-Effort Adaptation (BEA) bound. To make this approach practical for high-dimensional sequence policies, we develop scalable instance-level discrepancy proxies, stochastic alternating updates for policy and weights, and a multi-source extension that balances heterogeneous source domains. Across sim-to-sim, sim-to-real, and multi-source manipulation settings, BEACON improves robustness and data efficiency over target-only, fixed-ratio co-training, and feature-alignment baselines. Without an explicit alignment objective, BEACON also brings source and target representations closer together as an implicit result of discrepancy-aware co-training.
item.dc:creator: Antong Zhang, Han Qi, Heng Yang

item.title: RoboEvolve: Co-Evolving Planner-Simulator for Robotic Manipulation with Limited Data
item.description: arXiv:2605.13775v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The scalability of robotic manipulation is fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of task-aligned physical interaction data. While vision-language models (VLMs) and video generation models (VGMs) hold promise for autonomous data synthesis, they suffer from semantic-spatial misalignment and physical hallucinations, respectively. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboEvolve, a novel framework that couples a VLM planner and a VGM simulator into a mutually reinforcing co-evolutionary loop. Bootstrapped for self-evolution with unlabeled seed images, RoboEvolve leverages a cognitive-inspired dual-phase mechanism: (i) daytime exploration fosters physically grounded behavioral discovery through a semantic-controlled multi-granular reward, and (ii) nighttime consolidation mines "near-miss" failures to stabilize policy optimization. Guided by an autonomous progressive curriculum, the system naturally scales from simple atomic actions to complex tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RoboEvolve (I) achieves superior effectiveness, elevating base planners by 30 absolute points and amplifying simulator success by 48% on average; (II) exhibits extreme data efficiency, surpassing fully supervised baselines with merely 500 unlabeled seeds--a 50X reduction in initial RL data; (III) demonstrates robust continual learning without catastrophic forgetting; and (IV) extends to low-level control, improving cold-started LingBot-VA from 78.7% to 98.7% average task success on LIBERO using environment feedback. Together, these results demonstrate the applicability of our co-evolutionary framework to both internally supervised generative learning and environment-grounded action learning.
item.dc:creator: Harold Haodong Chen, Sirui Chen, Yingjie Xu, Wenhang Ge, Ying-Cong Chen

item.title: WorldArena 2.0: Extending Embodied World Model Benchmarking on Modality, Functionality and Platform
item.description: arXiv:2605.17912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World models have emerged as a central paradigm for embodied intelligence, enabling agents to predict action-conditioned future and reason about environmental dynamics. However, existing embodied world model benchmarks are still largely confined to vision-only prediction, offline embodied applications, and simulator-based evaluation, making them insufficient for assessing increasingly comprehensive world models. In this work, we introduce WorldArena 2.0, an expanded benchmark that systematically broadens embodied world model evaluation along three dimensions: modality, functionality, and platform. Along the modality dimension, WorldArena 2.0 extends evaluation from vision-only to visuotactile modalities, enabling assessment of multimodal perception and prediction. Along the functionality dimension, it extends beyond policy evaluation and planning to assess world models as interactive RL environments for policy optimization. Along the platform dimension, it moves beyond simulator-only evaluation to a diverse suite of simulated and real-world robotic settings across multiple embodiments. Under a standardized protocol, WorldArena 2.0 comprehensively evaluates perceptual quality, interactive utility, and cross-platform performance, providing a comprehensive testbed for tracking progress toward embodied world models. The project page including codes and demos is available at: https://world-arena.ai/.
item.dc:creator: Zhuohang Li, Yiding Ma, Yu Shang, Lei Jin, Shengyuan Wang, Jianjie Fang, Zhaolu Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Yinzhou Tang, Xin Jin, Ziyou Wang, Weikang Su, Xin Zhang, Haisheng Su, Weizhen He, Wei Wu, Haoyi Duan, Gordon Wetzstein, Xihui Liu, Dhruv Shah, Zhaoxiang Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhu, Yonghong Tian, Tat-Seng Chua, Xin Wang, Wenwu Zhu, Chen Gao, Yong Li

item.title: LLM-Guided Future Hypotheses for Horizon-Aware Exploration in Multi-Step Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2605.29864v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-step robot manipulation requires acting under uncertainty about how the scene will evolve, making exploration and policy adaptation challenging. We study whether short-horizon, task-consistent future videos can provide useful structured priors for control and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. We formalize this idea through Future-Experience Conditioning (FEC), a simple interface that conditions closed-loop policies on a latent representation of a short future video. In our simulation setup, future clips are generated in three stages, an LLM reasoner operating over a task ontology initialized from the current scene state, a robot-free digital-twin rollout of the intended object motion, and a mask-free video diffusion model that synthesizes a robot-consistent future clip without requiring segmentation at inference. We instantiate this future-conditioning interface primarily with BC and BC+RL, and compare against a future-conditioned Streaming Flow Policy (SFP) baseline on RoboCasa and CALVIN under NoFuture, GTFuture, GenFuture, and WrongFuture. Generated futures improve performance over no-future conditioning, while mismatched futures degrade it, and our BC+RL instantiation achieves the strongest overall results. An average BC+RL learning-curve analysis across 8 CALVIN tasks further shows that GTFuture improves fastest, GenFuture improves earlier and to a higher level than NoFuture, and WrongFuture remains at zero throughout training. These results suggest that short-horizon future videos can serve as useful structured priors for exploration and policy adaptation under imperfect future predictions. https://enact2026.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Andrew Melnik, Michael Beetz

item.title: CoMo3R-SLAM: Collaborative Monocular Dense SLAM with Learned 3D Reconstruction Priors for Outdoor Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.30488v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Outdoor robot teams need a shared dense map despite limited overlap, independent reference frames, and uncertain monocular scale. Collaborative dense SLAM systems typically resolve this with depth sensors, which add payload, power, and calibration cost. We present CoMo3R-SLAM, a collaborative monocular dense SLAM system that places learned feed-forward 3D reconstruction priors at the center of the multi-agent problem: their dense pointmaps anchor scale across agents and supply correspondences strong enough to verify inter-agent links geometrically. Each agent tracks and fuses its own keyframes from a single RGB stream, while a coordinator retrieves cross-agent keyframes over the prior's encoder features, verifies them by bidirectional dense pointmap matching, synchronizes the independent similarity gauges in closed form, and refines every keyframe in one unified multi-agent sim(3) graph. Finally, a pose-depth alternation over geometry-aware segments lets inter-agent observations constrain dense structure as well as trajectories. Requiring neither measured depth nor supplied intrinsics, CoMo3R-SLAM attains the lowest trajectory error on three of four Tanks and Temples scenes, and competitive accuracy on Waymo driving sequences, while running at approximately 6-8 FPS on RTX 3080 Ti. A long-horizon traversal, independently captured day and night streams, and teams of up to four agents further map its operating range.
item.dc:creator: Zhihao Cao, Qi Shao, Shuhao Zhai, Feng Tian, Anh Nguyen, Hesheng Wang, Baoru Huang

item.title: Haptic Sorter: A Unified Planning Framework for Online Shape Estimation and Real-Time Pose Inference
item.description: arXiv:2605.31352v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robotics manipulation usually assumes that the shape and pose of the object are known to the robot prior to motion planning. However, precise geometric information is not always available in practice, and pose inference suffers from sensor uncertainties and view occlusion. In this work, we propose a unified model-based geometric framework integrating robotic haptic perception, modeling, and manipulation planning. Our novelties involve: \textit{i)} Introducing Bayesian Optimization (BO) to guide the haptic exploration for object shape inference, where superellipses are used to approximate geometric boundary; \textit{ii)} Adaptive formulation of manipulation potential encoding object geometry for quasi-static robot-object interaction; \textit{iii)} Proposing an online Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) for real-time pose inference based on model prediction and tactile feedback. We deploy our system on a 2D robotic sorting task, and vary object geometries to validate the robustness and generalizability of our framework in both simulation and a real-world multi-arm setup.
item.dc:creator: Zhuoyi Lu, Lin Yang, Sri Harsha Turlapati, Domenico Campolo

item.title: Crazyflow: An Accurate, GPU-Accelerated, Differentiable Drone Simulator in JAX
item.description: arXiv:2606.01478v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-quality, large-scale synthetic data from simulations is becoming a cornerstone for pushing robots' capabilities. While aerial robotics simulators have evolved to support specialized needs such as fidelity, differentiability, and swarms independently, a unified platform that synthesizes data across all these domains is missing. In this work, we propose Crazyflow, a simulator designed to push the frontier of aerial robotics algorithm development, supporting model-based and data-driven methods, gradient-based and sampling-based approaches, single- and multi-agent systems, and state- and vision-based policy learning. Crazyflow combines high-fidelity dynamics with JAX for speed and differentiability, scaling to millions of environments or thousands of swarms with thousands of drones on single CPUs and GPUs, and beyond on clusters. Real-world experiments show Crazyflow supports both analytical-gradient-based policy learning, achieving high-accuracy tracking without domain randomization, and sampling-based obstacle avoidance at speeds exceeding half a billion steps per second. Breaking the traditional train-then-deploy paradigm, Crazyflow's performance enables in-flight reinforcement learning; we demonstrate this by throwing a physical drone into the air and training a recovery policy from scratch in 0.37 seconds, catching it before it hits the ground. By pushing accuracy, speed, and differentiability simultaneously, Crazyflow serves as an open-source resource for synthetic data generation, with emerging capabilities for large-scale parallelization for online, in-execution learning and optimization, opening the door to novel algorithm development.
item.dc:creator: Martin Schuck, Marcel P. Rath, Yufei Hua, Abhishek Goudar, SiQi Zhou, Angela P. Schoellig

item.title: Learning Action-Conditional and Object-Centric Gaussian Splatting World Models for Rigid Objects
item.description: arXiv:2606.01950v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World models enable intelligent agents to predict the consequences of their actions on the environment. In this paper, we propose Multi Rigid Object Gaussian World Model (MRO-GWM), a novel model that learns action-conditional dynamics of rigid objects in 3D. Using object-centric Gaussians, we can represent arbitrary object shapes and multi-object scenes. We develop a novel temporal-spatial transformer architecture that predicts future rigid body motion from a history of object Gaussians and future actions. Objects are represented by Gaussians in an object-centric frame, which allows to describe object motion as a rigid body transformation. Our model is trained on reconstructions from multiple viewpoints, which requires the model to also handle partial observations of objects due to occlusions. We analyze prediction performance of our approach on synthetic datasets composed of typical household objects with multi-object dynamics and interactions by a robot end effector. We also evaluate our model in model-predictive control for non-prehensile manipulation in simulation and for image-based tracking and prediction of object motion in simulated and real-world scenes.
item.dc:creator: Jens U. Kreber, Lukas Mack, Joerg Stueckler

item.title: PRISM: PRior-guided Imagination Sampling in world Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.07974v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent world models learn representations that enable them to predict how actions change the environment - a capability we call physical intuition. We find that these same representations also support action intuition: a lightweight head can learn a goal-conditioned action prior directly from the frozen encoder's features. We introduce PRISM to investigate how action intuition can be extracted from frozen world-model representations and used to guide goal-conditioned planning. The prior's mean and predicted uncertainty guide the search for useful actions, while the world model evaluates their consequences against the goal. Experiments on four simulated control tasks and two real-robot platforms show that a lightweight action head improves planning performance, and that the same fusion interface accepts a diffusion prior over the same frozen features without modification. These results demonstrate the potential of reusing world-model representations to both predict action consequences and guide action selection.
item.dc:creator: Yuhai Wang, Jiawei Xia, Bowen Sun, Rongxuan Zhou, Xiao Hu, Yongliang Shi, Jing Du, Yang Ye

item.title: MPPI-based Informative Trajectory Planning for Search and Capture of Drifting Targets with ASVs
item.description: arXiv:2606.12019v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) offer an efficient solution for environmental cleanup as well as search and rescue operations in open waters. Targets in these settings drift continuously, so efficient search must balance exploration of unobserved regions with tracking of known targets. However, most target tracking and pursuit scenarios consider simple guidance behaviours and short-term predictions for decision-making. In this letter, we address the problem of search and capture of multiple drifting targets, such as litter, in marine environments, using an adaptive informative planning approach. A key aspect of our strategy is a spatiotemporal informative planning method based on model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, a sampling-based model predictive control method. Our planner balances search and tracking objectives with a cost design that couples spatiotemporal target drift predictions and exploration objectives. The planner directly generates kinematic-level commands by optimising continuous trajectories over long horizons. In the interception stage, we use pure pursuit guidance for physical capture of the targets. Simulations show that our planner captures up to 18% more targets than the strongest baseline, proving its efficiency for environmental cleanup. Finally, we validate our approach in field trials with an ASV.
item.dc:creator: Sanjeev Ramkumar Sudha, Marija Popovi\'c, Erlend M. Coates

item.title: GeoHAT: Geometry-Adaptive Hybrid Action Transformer for Mobile Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2606.13394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation requires coordinating mobile base and manipulator under shifting viewpoints, posing challenges in geometric perception and action generation. Current policies either rely on 2D features or sparse 3D representations that lack dense spatial structure, and typically encode arm and base within one action vector that ignores their distinct control demands. Moreover, existing dense fusion strategies risk corrupting pretrained representations under noisy depth while incurring heavy computational overhead. We present GeoHAT, an end-to-end diffusion-based framework built on a simple principle: geometry should be injected only where reliable and attended to only where needed. GeoHAT employs a lightweight Fourier spatial encoder that maps dense per-pixel 3D coordinates into geometric tokens without an additional 3D vision backbone. These tokens are then selectively injected into vision foundation model features through per-token gated fusion modulated by depth validity, preserving the semantic prior while enriching spatial understanding. For action generation, a Hybrid Whole-Body Action Decoder decomposes arm and base into distinct subspaces and lets each action modality attend to its task-relevant visual context through sparse cross-attention, while causal temporal modeling captures intra-timestep coordination and inter-timestep dependencies. Experiments on the ManiSkill-HAB simulation benchmark demonstrate that GeoHAT achieves a 79.2% mean success rate, surpassing the strongest baseline by 23.6 pp. Furthermore, real-world experiments on diverse tasks also confirm consistent improvements over all baselines.
item.dc:creator: Xiangyu Zhu, Renjun Wu, Luzhou Ge, Jinyan Liu, Xuesong Li

item.title: LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies
item.description: arXiv:2606.15768v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining for semantic robot control, but often lack explicit foresight into how robot actions change the scene. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by conditioning policies on predicted futures, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive video generation with substantial pixel-level redundancy. We present LaWAM, a Latent World Action Model that exposes predictive dynamics to robot policies through compact latent visual subgoals instead of reconstructed future video. At the core of LaWAM is a latent-action-conditioned Latent World Model (LaWM). We obtain LaWM by training a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model and repurposing its forward decoder to predict future observation features for scene evolution. LaWAM then conditions action generation on these predicted latent visual subgoals to enable dynamics-aware robot control. LaWAM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive success rates (SRs) across LIBERO (98.6% SR), RoboTwin (91.22% SR), and real-world manipulation tasks while retaining low-latency inference. LaWAM runs in 187 ms per action-chunk prediction and achieves up to 24x lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.
item.dc:creator: Jialei Chen, Kai Wang, Kang Chen, Shuaihang Chen, Feng Gao, Wenhao Tang, Zhiyuan Li, Weilin Liu, Zhuyu Yao, Boxun Li, Yuanbo Xu, Chao Yu

item.title: ZiMPedance: Impedance-Aware ZMP Modeling and Control for Payload Carrying with Quadruped Robots
item.description: arXiv:2606.18883v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Load transportation with quadruped robots is strongly affected by the dynamics of the physical interface between the robot and the load. Passive spring-based arms provide a lightweight and mechanically compliant alternative to active manipulators, but their dynamics can store and release energy during locomotion, producing oscillatory interaction forces that reduce robot stability. This paper develops a passive-arm-aware ZMP model for a quadruped carrying a payload through a passive arm. The reduced analytical model relates passive-interface stiffness, damping, and payload mass to the ZMP response under both external payload forcing and locomotion-induced base excitation, showing that lightly damped passive modes can overlap with gait harmonics. We then propose an arm-aware MPC (ARMPC), a passive-arm Model Predictive Control approach based on extended Single Rigid Body Dynamics that combines reduced floating-base dynamics with passive-arm joint states, internal torsional springs and dampers, and base-arm inertial coupling. Simulation ablations show that ARMPC consistently reduces ZMP-margin violations and prevents failures across all tested conditions, while Nominal MPC, which neither models nor compensates the passive arm, and Baseline MPC, which compensates it through an estimated wrench, exhibit higher violation percentages and failures under disturbances. Hardware pull-release experiments with a 2 kg payload show that the proposed ARMPC completes all longitudinal and diagonal disturbance trials without failure, whereas Baseline MPC fails in 7/15 and 8/15 trials, respectively. The same model also enables passive-arm end-effector tracking while maintaining a positive ZMP margin.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni B. Dessy, Lorenzo Amatucci, Claudio Semini, Victor Barasuol

item.title: Plug, Play and Comply: Plugin-Based Compliant Control in ROS 2
item.description: arXiv:2607.22483v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper presents a robot-agnostic framework for implementing and deploying compliant-control algorithms across different manipulators.
